title: The Afternoon Brief: Liverpool changes hands, LIV Golf cuts $30M, Scheffler opens playoffs with eight-shot win
dek: A Bezos-linked consortium acquired 38% of Liverpool FC from Fenway Sports Group, while LIV Golf canceled its Michigan finale and halved prize money at this week's Indianapolis event as Saudi funding ends. Scottie Scheffler won the FedEx St. Jude Championship by eight shots to open the playoffs.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: The day pivots from morning's institutional change to midday's clearer picture of financial pressure and competitive dominance: Liverpool's ownership structure has shifted materially, LIV Golf's capital crisis is accelerating, and Scheffler has opened the postseason with a commanding statement.
bottom_line: Midday shifted from morning's institutional transitions to clearer pictures of financial pressure and performance. Liverpool's ownership has materially changed, with regulatory approval ahead and a 12-month option window determining whether the consortium takes control. LIV Golf's prize cuts and vendor unpaid invoices signal acute liquidity pressure as the Saudi PIF's funding ends; the BC Partners deal timeline is the critical checkpoint. Scheffler opened the FedEx Cup Playoffs with a dominant eight-shot win. The Welsh FA became the first home nation to withdraw backing for Infantino's re-election. Watch the Liverpool regulatory approval process, any movement on LIV's BC Partners financing or vendor litigation, and whether Infantino's re-election faces additional confederation pressure.
body: The morning's cascade of transitions continued through midday with ownership and funding news that sharpened focus on who controls which properties and how stable their financing truly is. The single clearest fact is Liverpool's ownership: a consortium named 1892 Holdings, led by British-Indian businessman Amit Bhatia and including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin, has acquired approximately 38% of the club from Fenway Sports Group under a definitive agreement, per the desk's reporting. The consortium holds an option to purchase a controlling stake within 12 months. The deal values Liverpool between £5bn and £6bn. Bhatia will become vice-chairman pending regulatory approval. The reporting does not specify the timeline for that approval or conditions FSG attached to the 12-month option window.

LIV Golf's financial trajectory tightened considerably midday. The league canceled its scheduled team championship in Michigan and cut prize money at this week's Indianapolis finale, reducing combined payouts by $30 million, as the desk reported. The Indianapolis individual competition will now pay out $10.1 million in total purses, down from a standard $20 million, with the winner's check dropping to $2.02 million from a typical $4 million. The canceled Michigan team championship was supposed to distribute $40.1 million to the league's 13 franchises. Originally, the two events were scheduled to pay out $70.1 million combined. The prize cuts follow the Saudi Public Investment Fund's April announcement to halt funding at season's end. Vendors and contractors report unpaid invoices ranging from several thousand dollars to nearly $100,000, with minimal response from the league's accounts receivable or legal departments. Mobii Systems Group Limited, a Canadian company that supplied LIV's streaming technology, claims the league owes it more than $1.1 million for breach of contract and unpaid invoices. The league is actively seeking new investment from BC Partners, but the reporting does not confirm a timeline for that capital infusion.

On the field, Scottie Scheffler won the FedEx St. Jude Championship by eight shots at TPC Southwind to open the FedEx Cup Playoffs, according to the desk's reporting. The victory came in a field competing to secure playoff standing and build momentum heading into the final FedEx Cup event.

In football governance, the Football Association of Wales chief executive Noel Mooney called for FIFA president Gianni Infantino to step down, citing damage from his attempted World Cup privatization plan. The FAW is now the first home nation to withdraw backing for Infantino's re-election bid, per the desk's reporting. Infantino's proposed structure would have created a new company to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all FIFA competitions with 21% of stakes sold to private investors; that plan has been scrapped.

In the Premier League, the league will publish the full verdicts of its Key Match Incidents Panel on referee and video assistant referee decisions for the first time this season, ending a policy of private judgment. The panel comprises five members: three former players and coaches, one Premier League representative, and one from Pro Ref, the referees' body. Until now, the panel's judgments have remained private, though clubs have periodically leaked the information.

In Australian football, the AFL Tribunal upheld Jacob van Rooyen's three-match suspension for a striking incident that rendered Port Adelaide's Aliir Aliir unable to continue playing. Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson rejected Melbourne's appeal and the club's submitted biomechanist evidence, calling it "not sufficiently probative, or really probative at all." Van Rooyen will miss Saturday's game against the Western Bulldogs and the Demons' first two finals.

In the WNBA, an overtime game between the Indiana Fever and Atlanta Dream on ESPN on August 17 drew 2.6 million average viewers and peaked at 4 million, the most-watched WNBA game on cable in history. Caitlin Clark scored 26 points and nine assists in the Fever's 95-91 win. The viewership figure represents a 178 percent increase from ESPN's average regular-season WNBA viewership last year.
